entry_json.own_context_sentence: Building new roads often exacerbates the congestion it was meant to relieve.
example_sentences: Cutting benefits exacerbated child poverty in the poorest districts.
Remote working may exacerbate inequality between office and manual staff.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Its object must already be a problem. You exacerbate poverty or tension, never a neutral thing.

entry_json.definition: the set of reasons behind a decision or belief
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The rationale behind the curfew was never explained to residents.
example_sentences: The rationale for the reform was to reduce administrative cost.
Critics accepted the rationale but questioned the timing.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Refers to a whole line of reasoning, so it is usually singular. Do not write 'many rationales' where you mean 'several reasons'.

entry_json.definition: a disadvantage of something that is otherwise useful
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main drawback of remote working is weaker informal contact.
example_sentences: Every proposed solution carries a drawback of some kind.
The obvious drawback is the cost of maintaining two systems.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Use when weighing advantages against disadvantages. For something harmful rather than merely inconvenient, use 'risk' or 'danger'.

entry_json.definition: the money available to a person, organisation or country
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Schools with limited financial resources cannot replace ageing equipment.
example_sentences: Financial resources should follow need rather than political influence.
Charities compete for the same shrinking financial resources.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Suits institutional contexts. For a household, 'income' or 'savings' is clearer than 'financial resources'.

entry_json.definition: as a result of what has just been mentioned
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fewer trains were running; consequently, roads became heavily congested.
example_sentences: The harvest failed and, consequently, prices rose across the region.
Consequently, the policy achieved the opposite of its stated aim.
entry_json.upgrade_note: A linking adverb, not a conjunction: use a full stop or semicolon before it, never a bare comma splice.

entry_json.definition: used to contrast two facts directly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Exports rose steadily, whereas imports fell for three consecutive years.
example_sentences: Older workers valued security, whereas graduates prioritised flexibility.
Reading scores improved, whereas writing scores remained unchanged.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Ideal for Task 1 comparisons of two data points. Both halves need a full clause with its own subject and verb.

entry_json.definition: in addition, and reinforcing what has just been said
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Furthermore, the scheme cost less than the campaign it replaced.
example_sentences: Furthermore, evening opening would benefit shift workers.
The plan is expensive; furthermore, it addresses only the symptoms.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Begins a new sentence adding a second supporting point. One per paragraph is plenty; a chain of them reads mechanically.

entry_json.definition: because of; as a result of
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Owing to poor weather, the harvest was delayed by a month.
example_sentences: Owing to rising costs, several projects were postponed indefinitely.
Attendance fell owing to the closure of the branch line.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Followed by a noun phrase, never a clause. Write 'owing to the delay', not 'owing to the train was late'.

lemma: a significant proportion of the population

entry_json.headword: a significant proportion of the population
entry_json.ipa: ə sɪɡˈnɪfɪkənt prəˈpɔːʃn əv ðə ˌpɒpjuˈleɪʃn
entry_json.definition: a notably large share of the people in a country or group
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A significant proportion of the population lives within reach of a station.
example_sentences: A significant proportion of the population has no savings at all.
Digital services exclude a significant proportion of the population.
A significant proportion of the population remains unaware of the scheme.
collocations: a significant proportion of the population
entry_json.upgrade_note: Takes a singular verb ('a proportion ... has'). Only use 'significant' where the share really is large; otherwise 'a small proportion'.

entry_json.definition: during the last twenty or thirty years
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In recent decades, family size has fallen across most of Europe.
example_sentences: In recent decades, manufacturing has given way to services.
Air travel has become far cheaper in recent decades.
collocations: in recent decades there has been
entry_json.upgrade_note: Pairs naturally with the present perfect for change over time. For the present situation only, use 'at present' or 'currently'.

entry_json.definition: young people in the years between childhood and adulthood
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Adolescents need considerably more sleep than school timetables allow.
example_sentences: Adolescents are particularly sensitive to comparison with their peers.
Screen use among adolescents has been studied intensively but inconclusively.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Suits academic and health contexts. In a friendly Speaking answer, 'teenagers' sounds more natural than 'adolescents'.

entry_json.definition: people who have reached retirement age
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Free travel for senior citizens reduces isolation as well as cost.
example_sentences: Senior citizens make up a growing share of the electorate.
Housing designed for senior citizens keeps them independent for longer.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Respectful and neutral. 'The elderly' is also accepted, but avoid 'old people' in formal writing.

entry_json.definition: to deal with a problem or subject in a serious way
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report addresses overcrowding but ignores its causes.
example_sentences: Any credible plan must address the shortage of trained staff.
The government has yet to address the underlying cause of the deficit.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Means to tackle a problem, not merely mention it. For simply discussing a topic, use 'discuss' or 'examine'.

entry_json.definition: to find out something definite by checking carefully
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Inspectors could not ascertain how long the fault had existed.
example_sentences: The survey sought to ascertain why patients missed appointments.
It is difficult to ascertain the true cost of the programme.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Formal and investigative, usually with 'whether' or a fact as its object. Not used for casually learning news.

entry_json.definition: to increase suddenly and sharply
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Demand for bicycles surged when fuel prices rose.
example_sentences: Applications surged after the fees were abolished.
Energy prices surged within a single quarter.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Only for sudden, steep rises in Task 1. For a gentle rise use 'climbed steadily' or 'rose gradually'.

entry_json.definition: to fall very quickly and by a large amount
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Passenger numbers plummeted when the service was reduced.
example_sentences: Sales plummeted in the final quarter of the year.
Confidence plummeted following the announcement.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Reserve it for dramatic falls; a small decrease should be 'dipped' or 'declined slightly'.

entry_json.definition: to discourage someone from doing something, usually by making it costly or difficult
entry_json.own_context_sentence: High fees deter capable students from applying at all.
example_sentences: Visible patrols deter opportunistic theft more effectively than cameras.
Complicated forms deter exactly the people the scheme should reach.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Followed by a person plus 'from' plus an -ing form. It means discourage, not physically prevent — for that use 'prevent'.

entry_json.definition: needing a lot of effort, skill or attention
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Nursing is physically and emotionally demanding work.
example_sentences: The course is intellectually demanding but well supported.
Caring for a relative is more demanding than most employers realise.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Use for work, roles and courses. For a problem that is hard to solve, use 'complex' or 'intractable'.

entry_json.definition: simple to understand or do, with no complications
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The application process is straightforward once the documents are gathered.
example_sentences: The solution is technically straightforward but politically difficult.
Registering online is relatively straightforward for confident users.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Best for processes and explanations. Its negative, 'far from straightforward', is a useful hedge in essays.

entry_json.definition: giving good value because it does not waste money or resources
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rail freight is far more economical than road haulage over long distances.
example_sentences: Smaller engines are more economical without being noticeably slower.
Buying in bulk is economical only if the food is actually eaten.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Means efficient value, not low price. For a low price alone, use 'inexpensive' — 'cheap' can imply poor quality.

entry_json.definition: far too high in price to be reasonable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Tenants are charged exorbitant fees simply to renew a contract.
example_sentences: Exorbitant childcare costs push parents out of the workforce.
The exorbitant price of insulin has been widely criticised.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Carries clear criticism of unfairness. For something merely costly, use 'costly' or 'prohibitively expensive'.

entry_json.definition: existing widely in a particular place or among a particular group
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Short-term contracts are especially prevalent in hospitality.
example_sentences: Obesity is more prevalent in areas with fewer sports facilities.
The practice remains prevalent despite repeated official warnings.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Used with 'in' or 'among' plus a group or place, typically for problems and conditions rather than pleasant things.

entry_json.definition: to correct something that is wrong or unsatisfactory
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Additional funding alone will not remedy the shortage of teachers.
example_sentences: The regulator ordered the company to remedy the safety failures.
Training can remedy weak literacy far later than was once assumed.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Use for situations, shortcomings and imbalances. For machines and objects, 'repair' is the natural verb.

entry_json.definition: to bring something under control and use its power usefully
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Coastal countries are beginning to harness tidal energy.
example_sentences: Schools could harness pupils' curiosity instead of suppressing it.
The scheme harnesses private investment for public infrastructure.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Its object should be a force or potential — energy, enthusiasm, data. Do not write 'harness a pen'.

entry_json.definition: to state something firmly as true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Campaigners assert that the consultation was never genuine.
example_sentences: The authors assert that the effect persists into adulthood.
It is often asserted, though rarely shown, that competition raises standards.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Implies a claim made without full proof, so it works well when you then challenge it. For neutral reporting use 'state'.

entry_json.definition: to become gradually worse in quality or condition
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Air quality deteriorated steadily as traffic volumes grew.
example_sentences: The building deteriorated rapidly once repairs were postponed.
Relations between the two authorities deteriorated over the funding dispute.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Intransitive — something deteriorates by itself. To say what caused it, use 'exacerbate' or 'worsen' with an object.

entry_json.definition: a harmful or unwanted result
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Night shifts have a well-documented adverse effect on health.
example_sentences: The charge had no adverse effect on trade in the city centre.
Researchers found an adverse effect on sleep but not on attainment.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Always with 'on' plus what is harmed. 'Adverse' collocates with effect, impact, consequences and conditions.

entry_json.definition: new and unlike anything done before
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The city trialled a novel approach to collecting food waste.
example_sentences: A novel solution is not automatically a better one.
The team developed a novel method for measuring the effect.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Means innovative, and is used before a noun. Do not use it for something merely recent — a novel car is not a new car.

entry_json.definition: in a way that is clearly noticeable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Attendance improved markedly after the free breakfast scheme began.
example_sentences: Results differ markedly between the two age groups.
The two cities differ markedly in how they fund transport.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Use where a difference or change is visible in the data. It modifies verbs and comparatives, not plain adjectives.
